study_identification.title: Atypical maturation of the functional connectome hierarchy in autism

study_characteristics.study_objective: To investigate maturational abnormalities in the cortical hierarchy among individuals with ASD by examining developmental trajectories of the principal functional connectivity gradient using normative modeling, and to explore how network-level connectomic disruptions mediate deviations in cortical hierarchy development.

imaging_modality.answer: T1-weighted MRI; T2-weighted MRI; Resting-state fMRI

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: HCP minimal preprocessing pipeline; QuNex (for ABIDE datasets); FreeSurfer for cortical surface reconstruction; Schaefer atlas with 200 parcels; Surface-based spatial smoothing 2mm FWHM; Bandpass filter 0.008-0.1 Hz

quality_checking_detail.answer: Participants with large head motion in rs-fMRI time series (≥ 0.5 mm mean framewise displacement) were excluded. Participants with faulty cortical surface segmentation in T1-weighted MRI were excluded. See Supplementary Fig. 1 for participant selection flowchart.

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: ComBat harmonization was applied to the gradient values to mitigate scanner and site effects within the ABIDE dataset. For normative modeling, intercepts were re-estimated for ABIDE dataset while retaining the nonlinear effect of age fixed from the HCP-D reference model.

response_variable.answer: Principal functional connectivity gradient values (200 ROIs from Schaefer atlas); Functional hierarchy score (cosine similarity between individual gradient and normative gradient)

predictor_effects.answer: Age and sex modeled with interaction term (age × sex); Nonlinear age effects modeled using P-splines. For longitudinal replication analysis, subject-specific random intercepts were included for parameters μ, σ, ν, and τ.

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The study explicitly addresses multiple nuisance structures: (1) Site effects handled through ComBat harmonization of gradient values and re-estimation of intercepts for new datasets; (2) Head motion controlled through exclusion criteria (mean FD ≥ 0.5mm) and sensitivity analysis including mean FD as covariate; (3) Age nonlinearity explicitly modeled using P-splines in GAMLSS; (4) Sex effects modeled through age×sex interaction; (5) Heteroscedasticity addressed by GAMLSS modeling variance (σ), skewness (ν), and kurtosis (τ) as functions of age; (6) Image quality controlled through exclusion of faulty cortical surface segmentation.

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The study does not perform explicit hold-out validation within the HCP-D training dataset. However, the study does evaluate model performance indirectly by examining whether 130 of 200 ROIs showed significant age effects (FDR-adjusted p<0.05), which provides some evidence that the model captures meaningful age-related variance. The study also examines distributional properties (skewness, kurtosis) of centile scores, though these are not formal validation metrics.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: When we fitted the functional gradients using the GAMLSS model, 130 of the 200 regions of interest (ROIs) showed significant changes with age (FDR-adjusted p-value (PFDR) < 0.05). (p.137, lines 137-138)

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: The normative model trained on HCP-D was transferred to the ABIDE-I dataset (discovery) and ABIDE-II dataset (replication), both representing independent samples within the same domain (children and adolescents with resting-state fMRI). The intercepts were re-estimated while retaining age-related nonlinear effects. This transfer learning approach with independent validation samples demonstrates same-domain independent validation.

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The study does not validate the normative model on data from different domains (e.g., different imaging modalities, different age ranges beyond the training range, different scanner types not included in training, or different populations). All datasets used (HCP-D, ABIDE-I, ABIDE-II) share the same domain: resting-state fMRI in children and adolescents aged 5-22 years. While there are site and scanner differences, these are within-domain variations rather than different-domain validation.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: No explicit text discusses validation on different domain datasets. All datasets are resting-state fMRI in similar age ranges: HCP-D (5-21 years), ABIDE-I and ABIDE-II participants within developmental stages.

clinical_groups_n.answer: ABIDE-I: ASD=333, TD=369; ABIDE-II: ASD=302, TD=355; ABIDE-II longitudinal subset: ASD=23, TD=15

clinical_groups_age.answer: ABIDE-I: ASD mean 13.91±3.58 years, TD mean 13.66±3.49 years; ABIDE-II: ASD mean 11.93±4.01 years, TD mean 11.36±3.20 years; ABIDE-II longitudinal: ASD mean 12.52±2.14 years at baseline, TD mean 13.34±1.82 years at baseline

deviation_metric.answer: Centile scores (age- and sex-specific indicators of deviations in gradient values); Functional hierarchy score (cosine similarity between individual's gradient and normative gradient for their age); Extreme scores indicate greater deviation from normal

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Two-sample t-tests comparing centile scores between ASD and TD groups; Linear models controlling for age and sex to compare gradient values between groups (implemented in BrainStat toolbox); Multiple comparisons corrected using FDR procedure; Age-bin analysis dividing participants into three developmental stages: childhood (5-12 years), early adolescence (12-15 years), and adolescents/young adults (15-22 years); Mediation analysis using lavaan R package with 5,000 bootstraps to examine whether participation coefficient (PC) centile scores mediated the relationship between diagnostic group and hierarchy score; Pearson correlation between hierarchy scores and SRS (Social Responsiveness Scale) total and subdomain scores (awareness, cognition, communication, motivation, mannerisms) to assess clinical relevance.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: ASD showed a non-linear developmental trajectory with delayed maturation in childhood, accelerated catch-up during adolescence, and subsequent decline in young adulthood; sensory and attention networks showed pronounced abnormalities in childhood while DMN impairment persisted throughout development; reduced DMN segregation mediated atypical cortical hierarchy development.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: The maturation of cortical hierarchy in individuals with ASD followed a non-linear trajectory, showing delayed maturation during childhood compared to TD individuals, followed by an accelerated 'catch-up' phase during adolescence (peak around 14.78 years for males and 14.98 years for females), and a subsequent decline in young adulthood. While TD individuals showed a nearly constant rate of increase (slope: 0.009/year ± 0.001/year for males and 0.0077/year ± 0.001/year for females), ASD individuals exhibited a steeper initial increase (slope: 0.013/year ± 0.033/year for males and 0.013/year ± 0.032/year for females). During childhood, significant network-level alterations were found in both low-level (somatomotor t=3.43 p=0.001; dorsal attention t=4.78 p<1e-4; ventral attention t=4.27 p<1e-4) and higher-order networks (DMN t=-5.67 p<1e-6). In early adolescence, only somatomotor (t=2.62 p=0.035) and DMN (t=-2.86 p=0.035) remained significant. In late adolescence and young adulthood, deviations were predominantly driven by decreased gradient values in DMN precuneus and posterior cingulate cortex (t=-3.72 p=0.002) and increased values in control network (t=2.88 p=0.016). Mediation analyses revealed that reduced DMN segregation was the only mediator of reduced hierarchy score in adolescence and young adulthood. Hierarchy scores correlated significantly with SRS total and all five subscores (average correlation -0.118 ± 5.96e-5), with highest correlation in communication subdomain, indicating that lower hierarchy scores (greater deviation from normative hierarchy) are associated with higher symptom severity. Variance analysis showed that TD group exhibited decreasing sigma with age (t=-2.415 p=0.016), indicating convergence to norms, while ASD group showed no such trend (t=0.047 p=0.96).
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: Small sample size particularly in older age range limited generalizability of findings during late adolescence and young adulthood; uncertainty in trajectory significantly increased at age extremes where data points are limited; linear trajectories observed in replication dataset (ABIDE-II) likely arose from age distribution imbalances; longitudinal datasets remain limited in ASD research with factors such as small sample sizes, short follow-up intervals, and demographic heterogeneity potentially influencing generalizability; use of GAMLSS for modeling nonlinear trajectories faces inherent challenges such as potential overfitting and complexity in interpretation; uneven distribution of samples across age groups limited ability to fully capture developmental trajectories among older individuals.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: The study suggests early interventions aimed at promoting normative development of higher-order networks may be critical for improving outcomes in individuals with ASD. The hierarchy score shows potential as a biomarker for identifying severity and progression of ASD. The observed transient alignment during early adolescence may contribute to decreased symptom severity during this stage, but symptoms could re-emerge or worsen during adolescence as cortical hierarchy deviates again from typical trajectories (compensation phenomenon). Future studies should prioritize datasets with well-balanced age distributions and implement rigorous sensitivity analyses. Extending this framework to other neurodevelopmental disorders (ADHD, schizophrenia) could provide comparative insights. Integrating genetic and molecular data could offer more comprehensive view of how aberrant neurobiological mechanisms contribute to functional abnormalities.

general_notes.general_notes: This study represents a comprehensive investigation of developmental trajectories in autism using advanced normative modeling with GAMLSS. Key methodological strengths include: (1) Large multi-site datasets (ABIDE-I: n=702, ABIDE-II: n=657, HCP-D: n=652); (2) Extensive replication analyses using independent ABIDE-II dataset; (3) Longitudinal validation subset (n=38); (4) Comprehensive sensitivity analyses including different parcellation schemes (Schaefer 200 vs Glasser 360), different connectivity thresholds (5%, 10%, 20%), handedness effects, and head motion control; (5) Novel whole-brain summary metric (hierarchy score) based on cosine similarity; (6) Integration of topological analysis (participation coefficient) with mediation framework to understand mechanistic pathways. The study also examined the second gradient (sensorimotor-visual axis) as supplementary analysis. Full demographic details are provided in Supplementary Tables 1-3, with site-specific imaging parameters in Supplementary Tables 4-5. The GAMLSS models four parameters: μ (mean), σ (variance), ν (skewness), τ (kurtosis), all as functions of age and age×sex interaction, using SHASH distribution. The study used 10% threshold for functional connectivity matrices (top 10% of connections retained per row). Combat harmonization was applied specifically to gradient values, not to raw BOLD data. The study carefully distinguished between cross-sectional age-related associations (described as 'maturational abnormalities' and 'developmental trajectories') and true longitudinal within-subject changes. Multiple datasets used: HCP-D for normative model training, ABIDE-I for discovery, ABIDE-II for replication, ABIDE-II longitudinal subset for longitudinal validation.
